subject: physics

items.q: Which objects emit infrared radiation?
items.correct: All objects, whatever their temperature happens to be
items.misconception: Only objects hot enough to glow red, orange or white
items.why: Infrared is introduced through hot objects - grills, heaters, thermal images of warm bodies - and 'radiates heat' sounds like something only a heat source can do. Thermal images of cold objects look dark, which students read as 'nothing coming out'. Emission never switches off. Temperature controls the rate, not whether it happens: the hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. A thermal camera can still form an image of a block of ice because the ice is emitting.
items.random_wrong: Only objects that are warmer than the air around them

items.q: Two identical metal blocks sit in the same room. Block X is at 80 °C and block Y is at 20 °C. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: X radiates more infrared each second than Y does
items.misconception: Only X radiates infrared, because Y is not hot at all
items.why: Infrared is introduced through hot objects - grills, heaters, thermal images of warm bodies - and 'radiates heat' sounds like something only a heat source can do. Thermal images of cold objects look dark, which students read as 'nothing coming out'. Emission never switches off. Temperature controls the rate, not whether it happens: the hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. A thermal camera can still form an image of a block of ice because the ice is emitting.
items.random_wrong: Y radiates nothing but absorbs the infrared from X

items.q: What is a perfect black body?
items.correct: An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it
items.misconception: An object whose surface is matt black rather than shiny
items.why: The name invites it, and black surfaces really are the best everyday absorbers, so the everyday meaning of 'black' is close enough to feel right. The definition is about behaviour, not colour: absorbs all incident radiation, reflects none, transmits none. It is an idealised model that real surfaces only approach.
items.random_wrong: An object that absorbs radiation and never emits any of it

items.q: Why would a perfect black body be the best possible emitter of radiation?
items.correct: A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter of it
items.misconception: It stores all the radiation it takes in and keeps it inside
items.why: 'Absorbing' sounds like storing, and insulation lessons teach that keeping energy in is a property of a surface. Students think of absorption and emission as opposites that cannot both be strong. Absorption and emission depend on the same surface property. A matt black car left in the sun gets hottest during the day and also cools fastest at night - the same surface is good at both.
items.random_wrong: Its black surface reflects radiation better than a shiny one

items.q: A book has been lying on a shelf in a cool room for several hours. Which statement about the book is correct?
items.correct: It is emitting infrared radiation and absorbing it as well
items.misconception: It is absorbing infrared radiation but is too cool to emit
items.why: Infrared is introduced through hot objects - grills, heaters, thermal images of warm bodies - and 'radiates heat' sounds like something only a heat source can do. Thermal images of cold objects look dark, which students read as 'nothing coming out'. Emission never switches off. Temperature controls the rate, not whether it happens: the hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. A thermal camera can still form an image of a block of ice because the ice is emitting.
items.random_wrong: It emits radiation only when it is warmer than the room

items.q: What does the emission from a body depend on?
items.correct: Its temperature, which sets both the intensity and the wavelengths
items.misconception: Its temperature, which sets the intensity but not the wavelengths
items.why: 'Hotter means more radiation each second' is the first rule students learn, and it is correct as far as it goes. Nothing in it hints that the mix of wavelengths changes too. Watch a heating element: it is invisible when warm, dull red when hotter, then orange. The wavelengths emitted have clearly changed, not only the amount.
items.random_wrong: Its temperature, which sets the wavelengths but not the intensity

items.q: A graph shows how the intensity of the radiation emitted by a body varies with wavelength, at 3000 K and again at 4000 K. Compared with the 3000 K curve, the 4000 K curve is:
items.correct: higher at every wavelength, with its peak at a shorter wavelength
items.misconception: the same height overall, with its peak at a shorter wavelength
items.why: Colour change is the visible effect, so it takes all the attention. On a graph, students notice the peak sliding sideways and overlook the whole curve rising. Compare two curves properly: the hotter curve lies above the cooler one at every wavelength as well as peaking further to the left. Both intensity and distribution respond to temperature.
items.random_wrong: higher at every wavelength, with its peak at the same wavelength

items.q: A central heating radiator is switched off and cools until it is at room temperature. Which statement is then correct?
items.correct: It still emits radiation, but less each second than before
items.misconception: It has stopped emitting radiation because it is not hot now
items.why: Infrared is introduced through hot objects - grills, heaters, thermal images of warm bodies - and 'radiates heat' sounds like something only a heat source can do. Thermal images of cold objects look dark, which students read as 'nothing coming out'. Emission never switches off. Temperature controls the rate, not whether it happens: the hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. A thermal camera can still form an image of a block of ice because the ice is emitting.
items.random_wrong: It now only absorbs the radiation coming from the warm air

items.q: A body stays at a constant temperature. What must be true?
items.correct: It absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits radiation
items.misconception: It has completely stopped absorbing and emitting radiation
items.why: 'Nothing changing' is read as 'nothing happening'. Students have not yet met the idea of a dynamic balance, where two opposite processes run at equal rates. Constant temperature is a balance, not a stop. The Earth's surface absorbs and emits enormous amounts of radiation every second while its temperature barely changes from day to day.
items.random_wrong: It emits radiation at a faster rate than it absorbs it

items.q: The temperature of a body is rising. Which statement describes what is happening?
items.correct: It is absorbing radiation faster than it is emitting radiation
items.misconception: It is emitting radiation faster than it is absorbing radiation
items.why: Hot objects do emit strongly, so students reverse cause and effect - the strong emission is the result of the high temperature, not the cause. The words 'radiating heat' make emission sound like heating. Track the direction of energy transfer. Radiation emitted leaves the body, so emitting faster than absorbing cools it; radiation absorbed arrives, so absorbing faster than emitting warms it.
items.random_wrong: It is absorbing radiation and is not emitting any radiation

items.q: Snow-covered ground reflects far more of the Sun's radiation than bare dark soil does. What is the effect of this?
items.correct: Less radiation is absorbed, so the ground stays colder
items.misconception: The reflected radiation warms the ground as it leaves
items.why: Students picture reflected radiation as staying inside the system. Diagrams draw the reflected arrow near the surface, which makes it look as though it lingers there. Only absorbed radiation transfers energy to a body. A reflected ray leaves for space; a snow-covered field reflects far more than dark soil does and so warms up much less in the same sunshine.
items.random_wrong: The ground absorbs the reflected radiation a moment later

items.q: Which statement about the factors that determine the temperature of the Earth is correct?
items.correct: It depends on the rates of absorption and emission, and on reflection
items.misconception: It depends only on how much radiation reaches the Earth from the Sun
items.why: The Sun is the obvious source, and everyday experience links sunshine directly with warmth. What leaves the Earth is invisible and easy to leave out of the account. Incoming radiation is only one side. How much is reflected straight back, how much is absorbed and how fast the Earth and its atmosphere emit back into space all matter, and the temperature settles where absorption and emission balance.
items.random_wrong: It depends only on how much radiation the atmosphere can trap in

items.q: A cup of tea is left in a room and slowly cools down. Using ideas about radiation, which statement is correct?
items.correct: It emits radiation faster than it absorbs it, so it cools
items.misconception: It absorbs radiation faster than it emits it, and so it cools
items.why: Hot objects do emit strongly, so students reverse cause and effect - the strong emission is the result of the high temperature, not the cause. The words 'radiating heat' make emission sound like heating. Track the direction of energy transfer. Radiation emitted leaves the body, so emitting faster than absorbing cools it; radiation absorbed arrives, so absorbing faster than emitting warms it.
items.random_wrong: It stops absorbing any radiation as soon as it begins to cool

items.q: A greenhouse warms up through the morning and then stays at a steady temperature all afternoon. Which statement about the afternoon is correct?
items.correct: It absorbs and emits radiation at equal rates, so it stays steady
items.misconception: It has stopped absorbing and emitting radiation, so it stays steady
items.why: 'Nothing changing' is read as 'nothing happening'. Students have not yet met the idea of a dynamic balance, where two opposite processes run at equal rates. Constant temperature is a balance, not a stop. The Earth's surface absorbs and emits enormous amounts of radiation every second while its temperature barely changes from day to day.
items.random_wrong: It cannot absorb any more radiation once it has stopped warming

items.q: A diagram shows radiation arriving at the Earth from the Sun and radiation leaving the Earth's surface. Which statement comparing them is correct?
items.correct: The Earth is much cooler, so it emits at longer wavelengths
items.misconception: The Earth sends back the same wavelengths that arrived at it
items.why: Arrows in and arrows out look alike on a diagram, and students who have not linked the emitted wavelengths to temperature have no reason to expect them to differ. Use the rule that the wavelength distribution depends on temperature. The Sun at thousands of degrees emits mainly visible and near-infrared; the Earth's surface, near 15 °C, emits longer-wavelength infrared - which is why atmospheric gases can absorb the outgoing radiation but not most of the incoming.
items.random_wrong: The Earth emits shorter wavelengths because its surface is solid

items.q: On a diagram of the Earth's energy balance, the surface is shown absorbing radiation at 168 W/m² and emitting radiation at 168 W/m². What does this tell you?
items.correct: The surface temperature stays constant while both continue
items.misconception: The surface has stopped absorbing and emitting radiation now
items.why: 'Nothing changing' is read as 'nothing happening'. Students have not yet met the idea of a dynamic balance, where two opposite processes run at equal rates. Constant temperature is a balance, not a stop. The Earth's surface absorbs and emits enormous amounts of radiation every second while its temperature barely changes from day to day.
items.random_wrong: The surface is warming, because it is absorbing radiation

items.q: An object only emits radiation if it is hotter than the air around it.
items.correct: Every object emits radiation all the time, whatever its surroundings are doing. Being cooler than its surroundings changes the balance between emission and absorption, not whether emission occurs.
items.misconception: Radiation only comes out of something when it is warmer than its surroundings - otherwise it just absorbs.
items.why: Students transfer the rule for conduction and convection, where net energy transfer needs a temperature difference, onto emission itself. Net cooling and emission get treated as the same thing. Separate the two rates. A cool object in a warm room is emitting and absorbing at the same time; it absorbs faster than it emits, so it warms up. Emission is happening throughout.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A perfect black body absorbs all radiation, so it never emits any.
items.correct: A perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it AND is the best possible emitter of radiation.
items.misconception: A black body swallows radiation and traps it, so nothing ever comes back out.
items.why: 'Absorbs everything' sounds final, and the phrase 'black hole' sits nearby in students' minds. Nothing in the word 'absorb' suggests the object is radiating at the same time. The specification pairs the two: since a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter. If it absorbed without emitting, its temperature would rise without limit, which does not happen.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Any body that is absorbing radiation must be getting hotter.
items.correct: The temperature of a body increases only when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation. A body can absorb steadily and still cool, if it is emitting even faster.
items.misconception: Absorbing radiation always warms something up.
items.why: Absorption is taught as energy going in, so it feels as though it must raise the temperature. The simultaneous emission is easy to forget. Only the difference between the two rates matters. A hot drink in a warm room is absorbing radiation from the room the whole time it cools, because it is emitting faster than it absorbs.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Gases in the atmosphere trap radiation, and that is the end of it.
items.correct: Gases in the atmosphere absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and then emit radiation themselves, some of it back towards the surface and some out into space.
items.misconception: The atmosphere works like a lid - radiation gets stuck under it and cannot get out.
items.why: The word 'trapped' is used loosely in everyday and even textbook language, and greenhouse diagrams often draw a barrier. Absorbing bodies being emitters too is the step that gets skipped. The atmosphere absorbs and emits, like any other body. It is a good absorber of infrared and therefore also a good emitter, and it is the radiation it emits back downwards that keeps the surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
